document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC in response to the Independent Market Monitor for PJM’s Answer et al

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al. 
 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities 
 
 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
 
     v. 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

MOTION FOR LEAVE AND ANSWER OF 
CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
Constellation1 moves for leave and submits this answer in response to the Independent 
Market Monitor for PJM’s answer2 to Constellation’s Request for Clarification, or in the 
Alternative, Request for Rehearing3 of the Commission’s December 18, 2025 Order.4 In relevant 
part, Constellation sought clarification that generators selling non-firm electricity to co-located 
large loads do not need to delist their capacity.5 The Commission should not force a generator to 
delist its capacity when the generator’s co-located load obligation is non-firm and service can be 
curtailed by both PJM and the generator. In such an arrangement, the generator’s output remains 
 
1 Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) submits this answer and motion for leave pursuant to 
Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213. 
Constellation respectfully submits there is good cause for the Commission to accept this answer as it is intended to 
aid the Commission in its decision-making. 
2 Answer and Motion for Leave to Answer of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM (Feb. 5, 2026) (“Market 
Monitor Answer”). Hereafter, the Independent Market Monitor for PJM is referred to as “Market Monitor.” 
3 Request for Clarification or, in the Alternative, Rehearing of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (Jan. 20, 2026) 
(“Clarification Request”). 
4 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“December 18th Order”). 
5 See Clarification Request at 2.

2 
 
available to the grid when needed to support resource adequacy. In opposing the request, the 
Market Monitor mischaracterizes Constellation’s position and misstates the law, facts, and record.6 
The Commission should reject the Market Monitor Answer, consistent with past practice.7   
First, the Market Monitor mischaracterizes the Clarification Request as “advocat[ing] for 
the ability to sell capacity twice.”8 That is wrong. The generator’s capacity would be sold only 
once – to PJM. The Market Monitor is conflating energy and capacity. They are not the same 
product. “Electric energy is the actual electricity that electric generators produce and which 
residential and business customers ultimately use. By contrast, electric capacity is the ability to 
produce [energy] when called upon.”9 The Clarification Request contemplated allowing existing 
generators to continue “serving”—that is, selling non-firm energy to—Co-Located Load without 
 
6 Market Monitor Answer at 2-7. 
7 The Commission prohibits answers to rehearing requests unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority. 18 
C.F.R. §§ 385.213(a)(2), 385.713(d)(1); see also PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,081, at P 27 (2025) 
(rejecting IMM answer to rehearing request); Indep. Mkt. Monitor for PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. v. Am. Elec 
Power Serv. Corp., 166 FERC ¶ 61,043, at P 8 (2019) (rejecting IMM answer to rehearing request). Unauthorized 
answers are only accepted if the Commission finds good cause to waive Rule 213(a)(2), e.g., if the unauthorized 
answer “provides … information … that … assist[s] in our decision-making process and [does] not cause undue 
delay.” Dominion Transmission, Inc., 163 FERC ¶ 61,128, at P 8 (2018). 
8 Market Monitor Answer at 4; see also id. at 3 (claiming that Constellation “asserts that even when capacity is sold 
to a data center that it can also sell the same capacity to PJM customers in the PJM capacity market”); id. at 2 
(“generators should not be permitted to sell capacity twice”) (capitalization removed); id. at 5 (“CEG proposes to 
extend the concept to mean that any generation owner could remove its capacity from the PJM Capacity Market by 
selling the capacity to a data center.”); id. (“CEG is not content to simply remove its capacity from the capacity 
market. CEG proposes to sell its capacity to a data center and also sell the same capacity for the same time period 
to the PJM market.”). 
9 PPL EnergyPlus, LLC v. Solomon, 766 F.3d 241, 247 (3d Cir. 2014) (internal citations omitted); see also Affirmed 
Energy, LLC v. FERC, No. 25-1091, Slip Op. at 42 (D.C. Cir. Feb. 10, 2026) (“Capacity is not actual electricity, but 
rather a ‘commitment to produce electricity or forgo the consumption of electricity’ in a future delivery year.”); 
Cent. Hudson Gas & Elec. Corp. v. FERC, 783 F.3d 92, 98 (2d Cir. 2015) (“[S]uppliers sell a commitment to produce 
electric energy if called upon to do so during a specified future time period, rather than electric energy itself.”); 
FERC, 
Understanding 
Wholesale 
Capacity 
Markets 
(last 
visited 
Feb. 
12, 
2026), 
https://www.ferc.gov/media/understanding-wholesale-capacity-markets (“A capacity market does not pay for the 
energy produced but instead pays for the ability to produce power when needed.”) (emphasis omitted).

3 
 
delisting as a capacity resource so long as “the capacity resource remains available to serve the 
grid when needed,”10 consistent with its obligations.  
Second, the Market Monitor suggests that such an arrangement is inconsistent with “[t]he 
obligations of capacity resources,” which “include the requirement to offer their full [capacity] in 
the energy and reserves markets every day.”11 But the Commission has previously clarified that 
PJM’s “must-offer requirement, when implemented, should not impede resources from exporting 
energy on a non-firm or recallable basis, i.e., that the must-offer requirement will not operate in 
[a] manner that requires the resource to sit idle.”12 Thus, a capacity resource is not required to sit 
idle by the phone 8,760 hours per year waiting to see if PJM might call.13 To the extent the 
generator can demonstrate that its obligation to provide energy to the co-located load is non-firm 
or recallable, and the load demonstrates that it will either curtail or be served by backup supply 
when generator and grid supply are unavailable, there is simply no reason for the generator to 
delist and exacerbate any supply shortfall. To the contrary, there is every reason for the 
Commission to encourage such arrangements, which allow new large loads to interconnect without 
 
10 Clarification Request at 1 (emphasis added). The Clarification Request also stated, “[a]s Constellation stated in its 
April 23, 2025 Reply Comments, ‘Constellation’s view is that any Existing Generation Capacity Resources that 
would prioritize serving co-located load over following PJM dispatch should instead seek removal of Capacity 
Resource status or otherwise seek appropriate replacement capacity to cover its capacity supply obligation.’” Id. at 
5 n.9 (quoting Constellation April 23, 2025 Reply Comments at 92-93). 
11 Market Monitor Answer at 4. 
12 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 139 FERC ¶ 61,057, at P 205 (2012). 
13 See generally PJM Manual 11, § 2.3.3.1 (stating Capacity Resource Offer Rules); Constellation April 23, 2025 
Reply Comments, Exhibit 2 at 46:7-14 (Testimony of Zachary Ming) (“For any generator to participate in the 
capacity market, it is expected to provide output to the grid when system conditions require and when ordered to by 
PJM. If a co-located generator clears in the capacity market, this means that, at a minimum, it must output to the 
grid when needed or face performance penalties, even if that means interruption of the co-located load, either through 
curtailment or backup generation. I agree with PJM’s statement that ‘no portion of a committed Capacity Resource 
(whether composed of one or multiple physical generating units) may prioritize serving load that PJM is not 
responsible for serving.’”) (citations omitted).

4 
 
impacting resource adequacy. The Clarification Request seeks nothing more than the same type of 
treatment already afforded non-firm exports.14 Constellation acknowledges that there may have to 
be adjustments to the energy offer price rules to accommodate the non-firm supply of co-located 
load from a capacity resource. Adjustments to energy offer price rules have occurred from time to 
time over the years15 and Constellation is not advocating for a “radical change in the structure of 
PJM markets.”16   
Third, the Market Monitor asserts that the Clarification Request proposed to “remove … 
capacity from the capacity market.”17 The Clarification Request proposed the exact opposite. 
Constellation sought clarification to avoid a scenario where a capacity resource that remained 
available to serve the grid when needed would be forced to delist and “needlessly remove available 
capacity from serving the grid.”18 
Fourth, the Market Monitor incorrectly states “[t]he Commission has not approved” “that 
existing generating capacity and its energy output can be sold directly to a data center, outside 
PJM markets….”19 The Commission expressly contemplated this scenario and, to effectuate it 
efficiently, “direct[ed] PJM to file Tariff changes” addressing “an Interconnection Customer 
 
14 Clarification Request at 1. 
15 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 126 FERC ¶ 61,145, order on clarification, 127 FERC ¶ 61,188 (2009) 
(directing PJM to propose an approach for addressing the incorporation of opportunity costs in mitigated offers). 
16 Market Monitor Answer at 2. 
17 Id. at 6.  
18 Clarification Request at 1.  
19 Market Monitor Answer at 2.

5 
 
seeking to serve Co-Located Load using an existing generating facility….”20 If the Market Monitor 
disagreed, it should have sought timely rehearing of the December 18th Order.21 
Finally, the Market Monitor provides no substantive support for its bald assertion that 
Constellation’s “request for clarification on jurisdiction issues is not just and reasonable and should 
be denied.”22 The Market Monitor neither specifically mentions nor engages with Constellation’s 
request that the “Commission … clarify that it did not intend to change the scope of its jurisdiction 
over a generator’s wholesale sales and transmission.”23 As such, the Market Monitor’s assertion 
should be disregarded.   
CONCLUSION 
For the foregoing reasons, the Commission should reject the Market Monitor Answer as it 
fails to comply with Rule 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure and cannot 
support the Commission in its decision making.
